findings.title: app.shutdown(...) is not refused inside a registration watcher (only ServerHandle.shutdown is)
findings.description: RegistrationListener's Javadoc says a watcher must not shut down the app (IllegalStateException), and the SEC-APP-002 trace note says requireNotWatching guards shutdown. In fact only the anonymous ServerHandle.shutdown (line 627, also mis-indented) calls RegistrationLog.requireNotWatching(); RestApp.shutdown(long, TimeUnit) at line 729 has no guard, and none of its other entry points do either. Scenario 1 (NEW): a watcher calls app.shutdown(0, SECONDS) while it decides on app.get("/w", h). terminateIfNew moves the app to TERMINATED and closes the logger, the watcher returns normally, and the registration is then applied and recorded on a terminated app with no exception. Scenario 2 (RUNNING, registering thread is not a request thread): beginStop runs the stop sequence on this thread, which waits for in-flight requests while it holds the app monitor and the JVM-wide RegistrationLog.LOCK. Any in-flight request that registers (an app route, or a route on a Router mounted anywhere) blocks on LOCK, so the stop waits for the full timeout. The earlier w01 prickly HIGH (watcher could listen/freeze/shutdown) was fixed for only one of the two shutdown entry points.
findings.suggested_fix: Call RegistrationLog.requireNotWatching() first in DefaultRestApp.shutdown(long, TimeUnit), so the handle path is covered through delegation, and drop the duplicate in the handle. Add a test beside SEC_APP_002_AC5_watcherCannotListenOrFreezeMidRegistration that calls t.app().shutdown(...) from a watcher and expects ISE and state NEW.

findings.title: User watcher code runs under the JVM-global RegistrationLog.LOCK (and the app monitor), so registrations serialize across all apps and can deadlock
findings.description: LOCK is a static Object shared by every app and Router in the JVM. admit() and admitRouterLocked() call every RegistrationListener.onRegistration while holding it, and the app monitor too. A watcher is arbitrary user code (auth's protectOnly watcher, logging, I/O), and the lock serializes every registration of every app in the process behind it, including post-listen route/use/mount registrations. Concrete deadlock: thread T1 registers on app A, so its watcher runs holding A's monitor and LOCK. The watcher calls any synchronized config method of another app B, for example b.onRegistration(...), b.trustProxyHops(..) or b.ws(..), even one that would only throw ISE, and blocks taking B's monitor. Meanwhile T2 registers on a Router mounted in B: admitRouter takes B's monitor (holding()) and then waits for LOCK. Neither thread can continue, and there is no timeout. A watcher that waits for a Future doing a registration on another thread deadlocks the same way. The Javadoc forbids only registering from the watcher thread itself.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a per-app lock instead of the static LOCK, or at least do not hold LOCK while calling watchers: snapshot listeners, validate, and call watchers under the app monitor only, then take LOCK for apply+record (re-checking the Router's mounts as admitRouter already does). Document in RegistrationListener that the watcher must not block or touch another app.

findings.title: Monitor ordering by System.identityHashCode has no tie-break, so a hash collision gives a lock-order inversion
findings.description: owners() sorts the mounting apps by identityHashCode only. Collections.sort is stable, so apps with equal hash codes keep the order of router.mounts. Router R1 mounted in A then B and Router R2 mounted in B then A, with identityHashCode(A)==identityHashCode(B) (rare but possible, since identity hashes are not unique), give T1 (R1 registration) locking A then B and T2 (R2 registration) locking B then A: a classic deadlock with no timeout.
findings.suggested_fix: Give each RegistrationLog a unique long sequence number (static AtomicLong) and sort owners by it, or use it as the tie-break.

findings.title: A shared Router keeps strong references to every app it was ever mounted in
findings.description: record() adds a Mount(log, record) to router.mounts for each ROUTER_MOUNT. A Mount pins the app's RegistrationLog, its owner (the DefaultRestApp) and all its records. Mounts are pruned only lazily in owners(), which runs only when a later registration is made through that Router, and only for TERMINATED apps. A static or shared Router mounted into many short-lived apps (per-test apps, hot-reload or per-tenant app factories, apps that fail before listen and are never shut down, which stay NEW forever) therefore retains every such app indefinitely once the Router stops receiving registrations.
findings.suggested_fix: Prune terminated mounts on app termination (AppLifecycle callback removing its Mounts under LOCK), or hold the log through a WeakReference in Mount.

findings.title: Dispatcher/DefaultRequest still carry the legacy trustProxy boolean that is immediately overwritten by proxyTrust(..)
findings.description: Dispatcher keeps `private final boolean trustProxy` and passes it into every DefaultRequest constructor, then calls req.proxyTrust(proxyTrust) right after. DefaultRestApp.freeze (lines 1186-1190) passes proxyTrust.legacyFlag() to the constructor and then calls dispatcher.proxyTrust(proxyTrust) on a field that was just constructed. That makes two sources of truth, plus a volatile post-construction setter on a hot per-request object. A future construction site that forgets proxyTrust(..) silently falls back to legacy/none and drops hop/CIDR mode. Carried open item from w01 prickly review.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass ProxyTrustSetting through the Dispatcher and DefaultRequest constructors (final field) and delete the boolean parameter and the setters.

findings.title: HttpRoutes.terminal now instantiates a public class from the internal package
findings.description: The public default method HttpRoutes.terminal (HttpRoutes.java:51) returns `new com.snoworca.naruserve.internal.TerminalMiddleware(callback)`, so TerminalMiddleware and its public constructor become part of the published NaruServe-api jar surface that user code can reference. Its package-private `handler` field is read by RegistrationLog.routeTarget for record targets. Carried open item from the w01 prickly review (same pattern as AsyncMiddleware).
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the class but make the constructor reachable only through a package-private factory, or move the record-target unwrapping behind an internal interface that the default method's lambda implements.

findings.title: AdminEndpoints is ~1,300 lines with one class handling users, groups, keys, guards and JSON
findings.description: Deferred L16 (w06): the class has grown to 1,303 lines. It mixes the scope guards, A1-A6 users with the multi-step A4 PATCH state machine, G1-G8 groups with the R31 enumeration, key endpoints and the JSON/body helpers. That makes the security-relevant paths (keyBodyFirst, checkPatch recheck, protectAffected) hard to review in isolation.
findings.suggested_fix: Split into UserAdminEndpoints, GroupAdminEndpoints and KeyAdminEndpoints with a shared EndpointSupport for guards and body/JSON helpers.

findings.title: Duplicated helpers between AccountEndpoints and AdminEndpoints
findings.description: Deferred (w08): continueLater (AccountEndpoints 175-182 vs AdminEndpoints 327-334), checkNewPassword vs newPassword (161-173 vs 1164-1176), body(req) (122-128 vs 1230-1240, the Admin one also honours BODY_ERROR), string(..) helpers and the hash-slot submit + wipe + continueLater pattern (hashThen vs the inline blocks in createUser/patchUser) are copied. A fix to one copy, for example wiping or the BODY_ERROR replay, does not reach the other.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the helpers into one package-private EndpointSupport used by both classes.

findings.title: API key lastUsedAt is recorded at verification, before the endpoint/middleware may refuse the key
findings.description: Deferred (w08): verify() calls auth.apiKeyUsage().used(k.getId()) as soon as the key verifies. The middleware then refuses key credentials on some paths, for example 403 api_key_not_allowed on /auth/me/apikeys, /auth/password or an anonymous-entry endpoint. Such a refused request still bumps the key's lastUsedAt, so the admin key list reports the key as used even though no request with it succeeded. That misleads stale-key cleanup decisions.
findings.suggested_fix: Return the key id in the Credential and record usage only once the middleware has accepted the principal for the route (or after the response status is < 400).

findings.title: Two user-store reads per ver++ and a stale-deletion entry dropped on executor rejection
findings.description: Deferred (w10): bump() reads the owner in bumpInLock (findById at 210, or 199 on the busy path) and again in afterBump (171), plus keys.listByOwner. That makes two user-store reads for every logout?all, password change, disable or recovery. On RejectedExecutionException, scheduleStale removes staleVers[ownerId] and only WARNs. The stale keys then stay until a request presents one of them, and afterBump's 'next request schedules it again' covers only keys that are used.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass the ver re-read in bumpInLock to afterBump (ver+1 after a true write) instead of re-reading. On rejection, leave the work to the R42 cleanup run, for example by adding the owner to a retry set that cleanupRun drains.
